title: Oil Surges Past $100 as Houthi Attacks on Saudi Tankers Open Second Front in Iran War
excerpt: Brent crude breaks triple digits for the first time since May after Yemen's Houthis strike two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, threatening to shut a critical alternative shipping route.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Brent crude oil surged 7% past $100 after Houthi attacks on Saudi tankers.
  • The Bab el-Mandeb Strait is threatened, risking 24% of global oil supply.
  • Goldman Sachs predicts Brent could hit $120 in Q4 if disruptions continue.
  • Indian refiners suspended Iraqi crude loadings due to shipping risks.
  • U.S. gasoline prices reached $4.09 per gallon, 37% above pre-war levels.

Brent crude oil shattered the $100-a-barrel mark on Thursday for the first time since May, rising more than 7% after Iran-backed Houthi forces attacked two Saudi Arabian oil tankers in the Red Sea and opened a dangerous new chapter in the widening Middle East conflict.

The Houthis, who control northern and western Yemen, claimed responsibility for striking the tankers Encelia and Layla in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Saudi state media confirmed one vessel caught fire. The attacks came just three days after the group announced a naval blockade on Saudi shipping through the narrow waterway.

A Second Chokepoint Under Threat

The Bab el-Mandeb Strait has served as a critical alternative route for Saudi oil exports after Iran’s effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz disrupted Gulf shipping. A simultaneous blockade of both waterways could obstruct roughly 24% of global oil supply, according to the Council on Foreign Relations.

https://x.com/EconomicTimes/status/2080289939720372231

“The escalation compounds the near-halt in Hormuz traffic and the sharp reduction in Iranian exports, intensifying concerns over near-term global availability.”

— Gelber and Associates

Brent crude for September delivery settled at $100.69 a barrel, its highest close since May 22. U.S. benchmark West Texas Intermediate climbed 6.2% to $92.19. The rally has driven prices up roughly 20% in two weeks.

Trump Threatens ‘Major Military Punishment’

President Donald Trump responded with escalatory language, posting on Truth Social that the United States would “hold Iran responsible” for any future Houthi strikes and that “major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran and, of course, the Houthis, themselves.”

Speaking to Axios, Trump said he was considering relaunching major combat operations against Iran and was close to a decision. “They haven’t received enough pain yet,” Axios quoted him as saying.

The U.S. military has conducted 12 consecutive nights of air strikes against Iranian targets. Iran responded by firing at neighboring Arab countries that host American bases. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards declared the Strait of Hormuz “completely closed” while U.S. operations continued, warning no tanker would pass without coordination with Tehran.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a diplomatic gathering in Southeast Asia that the price Iran pays “will get higher every night” until Tehran agrees to a lasting peace deal.

Ripple Effects Across Global Markets

Goldman Sachs warned Brent could exceed $120 a barrel in the fourth quarter and average $100 next year if the Hormuz disruption persists through 2027, with further upside if the Bab el-Mandeb and Suez Canal also suffer prolonged blockades.

U.S. gasoline prices have reached $4.09 per gallon, 37% above the pre-war average of $2.98, according to AAA. Shipping rates have surged as tankers reroute around Africa, adding weeks to delivery times and reducing available global fleet capacity.

The supply crisis has widened beyond the Middle East. Kazakhstan has cut production after drone attacks shut down tanker loadings at a Black Sea terminal. Russian fuel exports remain constrained by Ukrainian strikes on refineries.

Global Oil Supply Under Threat
›24% of global oil supply at risk from Bab el-Mandeb blockade.
›Simultaneous closure of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb could disrupt oil exports.
›Kazakhstan cut production due to Black Sea terminal attacks.
›Russian fuel exports constrained by Ukrainian strikes.

India Feels the Squeeze

Indian state refiners have suspended Iraqi crude loadings due to shipping risks through the Strait of Hormuz, adding strain to an economy that imports more than 80% of its oil. India had already been grappling with a weakening rupee near record lows as the oil surge widens the country’s current account deficit.

For millions of Indian households — and diaspora communities connected to them — sustained triple-digit oil prices threaten higher food and fuel costs, eroding purchasing power and remittance value.

What’s Next

Markets are bracing for further escalation. Two Chinese supertankers carrying 4 million barrels of Saudi oil managed to exit the Red Sea via the Bab el-Mandeb on Thursday, according to shipping data — a sign that passage remains possible but increasingly risky. Traders and governments alike will be watching to see whether the Houthis enforce their blockade selectively or attempt to choke all Saudi exports.

Impact on India
›Indian refiners suspended Iraqi crude loadings due to risks.
›India imports over 80% of its oil.
›Weakened rupee exacerbates current account deficit.
›Higher oil prices threaten food and fuel costs for households.
